rationale: B wins because it keeps the story inside the facts and sharpens the actual tension: "Sweetgreen says its automated stores earn more. The margin comes as a range, not a number." A has good bones, but "The $15 salad is now assembled by robot" invents a price point and then builds a wobbly premium-category thesis on top of it. B is the set a founder can actually use without first scraping off the showmanship.
gaps_in_A: "The $15 salad" is not in the update. Cute line, bad discipline.
"premium, customizable, ingredient-forward) was supposed to be the tier where automation couldn't go" is an asserted market belief, not a supplied fact.
"ongoing fights around restaurant-worker protections and minimum wage" is an outside backdrop the update did not provide. That is how fake pegs sneak in wearing a decent jacket.
"McDonald's, Chipotle's Autocado, etc." may belong in later reporting, but dropping competitors into the proof list risks turning a Sweetgreen rollout into an unsupported rivalry frame.
gaps_in_B: "automated stores earn more" is loose. The update says higher restaurant-level margins, not earnings.
"a regional paper with Sweetgreen stores" is too broad unless tied to an actual retrofit market or local workforce impact.

"a company statement on how the automated-store margin relates to the path to net profitability" is necessary but not enough; the investor angle also needs analyst or filing validation because the margin claim is self-reported.
"That reporter will write this story with or without the company" is useful pressure, but it overstates certainty. Keep the warning, lose the clairvoyance.
